claim: Self-motion signals are distributed ubiquitously across parietal-temporal lobes.
source: Self-motion signals, distributed ubiquitously across parietal-temporal lobes, propagate to limbic hippocampal system for vector-based navigation via hubs including posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) and retrosplenial cortex (RSC).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a background claim.

claim: Self-motion signals propagate to limbic hippocampal system for vector-based navigation via hubs including posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) and retrosplenial cortex (RSC).
source: Self-motion signals, distributed ubiquitously across parietal-temporal lobes, propagate to limbic hippocampal system for vector-based navigation via hubs including posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) and retrosplenial cortex (RSC).
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the abstract and supported by the study design.

claim: Robust vestibular responses were discovered in PCC when macaques were provided translation and rotation stimuli on a 6-degree-of-freedom motion platform.
source: Providing translation and rotation stimuli to macaques on a 6-degree-of-freedom motion platform, we discovered robust vestibular responses in PCC.
evidence: This is a primary finding directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: A combined three-dimensional spatiotemporal model captured PCC data well.
source: A combined three-dimensional spatiotemporal model captured data well and revealed multiple temporal components including velocity, acceleration, jerk, and position.
evidence: This is supported by model fitting results shown in Figures 7-10.

claim: The spatiotemporal model revealed multiple temporal components including velocity, acceleration, jerk, and position in PCC neurons.
source: A combined three-dimensional spatiotemporal model captured data well and revealed multiple temporal components including velocity, acceleration, jerk, and position.
evidence: This is supported by the PVAJ model fitting results shown in Figures 9-10.

claim: RSC contained moderate vestibular temporal modulations compared to PCC.
source: Compared to PCC, RSC contained moderate vestibular temporal modulations and lacked significant spatial tuning.
evidence: This is supported by the proportion of temporally tuned neurons shown in Figure 4A and Table 1.

claim: RSC lacked significant spatial tuning.
source: Compared to PCC, RSC contained moderate vestibular temporal modulations and lacked significant spatial tuning.
evidence: This is supported by the spatial tuning analysis shown in Figure 4A and Table 1.

claim: Visual self-motion signals were much weaker in both PCC and RSC regions compared to the vestibular signals.
source: Visual self-motion signals were much weaker in both regions compared to the vestibular signals.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of visual and vestibular responses shown in Figure 12 and Table 1.

claim: Macaque posterior cingulate region carries vestibular-dominant self-motion signals with plentiful temporal components that could be useful for path integration.
source: We conclude that macaque posterior cingulate region carries vestibular-dominant self-motion signals with plentiful temporal components that could be useful for path integration.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Landmark-based and vector-based navigation are two commonly used strategies for spatial tasks.
source: In cognitive studies, landmark-based and vector-based navigation are two commonly used strategies for spatial tasks (Gallistel, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Vector-based navigation involves momentary self-motion cues from multiple sensory channels such as optic flow and vestibular ones for updating and accumulating one's heading direction and location.
source: Vector-based navigation, or path integration on the other hand, involves momentary self-motion cues from multiple sensory channels such as optic flow and vestibular ones for updating and accumulating one's heading direction and location (Etienne and Jeffery, 2004; Valerio and Taube, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Linear and angular vestibular signals originating from peripheral otolith and semicircular canal organs are thought to provide critical inputs to head direction cells, place cells or grid cells in the hippocampal-entorhinal navigation system.
source: For example, linear and angular vestibular signals originating from peripheral otolith and semicircular canal organs are thought to provide critical inputs to head direction cells (HD cells), place cells or grid cells in the hippocampal-entorhinal navigation system (Knierim et al., 1998; Stackman et al., 2002; Clark and Taube, 2012; Hitier et al., 2014; Jacob et al., 2014; Winter et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: Robust vestibular and visual signals related with self-motion have been discovered in numerous cortical areas including MSTd, VIP, VPS, PIVC, FEFsem, and 7a.
source: To date, robust vestibular and visual signals related with self-motion have been discovered in numerous cortical areas including the dorsal part of medial superior temporal sulcus (MSTd) (Duffy and Wurtz, 1997; Page and Duffy, 2003; Gu et al., 2006), the ventral intraparietal area (VIP) (Bremmer et al., 1999; Bremmer et al., 2002; Zhang and Britten, 2004; Chen et al., 2011a; Chen et al., 2011b), the visual posterior sylvian area (VPS) (Chen et al., 2011c), parietal insular vestibular cortex (PIVC) (Grüsser et al., 1990a, Grüsser et al., 1990b; Chen et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2011b), the smooth eye movement of the frontal eye field (FEFsem) (Gu et al., 2016), and 7a (Avila et al., 2019), composing a network (Guldin and Grüsser, 1998; Britten, 2008; Cheng and Gu, 2018; Gu, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Most cortical self-motion areas (except for 7a) have not shown direct connections with the hippocampal navigation system.
source: However, most of these areas (except for 7a) have not shown direct connections with the hippocampal navigation system.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge based on existing literature.

claim: PCC and RSC may be one of the hubs bridging the cortical self-motion system and the limbic hippocampal navigation system.
source: One hypothesis is that PCC and RSC may be one of these hubs (Rushworth et al., 2006; Vincent et al., 2010; Kravitz et al., 2011).
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: PCC and RSC directly project to entorhinal and parahippocampal cortices.
source: On one hand, there is evidence that PCC and RSC directly project to entorhinal and parahippocampal cortices (Rosene and Van Hoesen, 1977; Vogt et al., 1979; Insausti et al., 1987; Vogt et al., 1987; Morecraft et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by multiple anatomical tracing studies cited.

claim: PCC and RSC are heavily connected with cortical areas including area 7a, MSTd, FEF, PIVC, VPS and 3a.
source: On the other hand, these areas are also heavily connected with cortical areas including area 7a (Pandya et al., 1981; Vogt et al., 1987; Musil and Olson, 1988; Cavada and Goldman-Rakic, 1989; Olson and Musil, 1992; Shinder and Taube, 2010), MSTd (Akbarian et al., 1994; De Castro et al., 2020), FEF (De Castro et al., 2020), PIVC, VPS and 3a (Guldin and Grüsser, 1998; De Castro et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple anatomical connectivity studies cited.

claim: Navigation related neurons in PCC are reported when monkeys navigate in a virtual environment.
source: For example, navigation related neurons in PCC are reported when monkeys navigate in a virtual environment (Sato et al., 2006; Sato et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Lesion studies confirmed that PCC in monkeys and the homologues area in rodents were actively involved in spatial memory tasks.
source: Lesion studies confirmed that PCC in monkeys (Sutherland et al., 1988; Murray et al., 1989) and the homologues area in rodents were actively involved in spatial memory tasks (Sutherland et al., 1988; Cooper et al., 2001; Cooper and Mizumori, 2001; Whishaw et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to lesion studies.

claim: Vestibular signals were discovered in human PCC using functional MRI with galvanic or caloric stimulation.
source: Using functional MRI with galvanic or caloric stimulation, vestibular signals were discovered in human PCC (Smith et al., 2012; Schindler and Bartels, 2018), and visual signals were reported in human and macaque PCC (Wall and Smith, 2008; Fischer et al., 2012; Cottereau et al., 2017; Smith et al., 2017; Schindler and Bartels, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to fMRI studies.

claim: Visual signals were reported in human and macaque PCC.
source: Using functional MRI with galvanic or caloric stimulation, vestibular signals were discovered in human PCC (Smith et al., 2012; Schindler and Bartels, 2018), and visual signals were reported in human and macaque PCC (Wall and Smith, 2008; Fischer et al., 2012; Cottereau et al., 2017; Smith et al., 2017; Schindler and Bartels, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to imaging studies.

claim: HD cells have been reported in rat RSC.
source: For example, HD cells have been reported in rat RSC (Cullen and Taube, 2017), and inactivation of RSC disrupts HD cell and place cell activities in hippocampal circuit (Cooper and Mizumori, 2001; Clark et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous studies.

claim: Inactivation of RSC disrupts HD cell and place cell activities in hippocampal circuit.
source: For example, HD cells have been reported in rat RSC (Cullen and Taube, 2017), and inactivation of RSC disrupts HD cell and place cell activities in hippocampal circuit (Cooper and Mizumori, 2001; Clark et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to inactivation studies.

claim: In human, RSC is active in virtual navigational tasks.
source: In human, RSC is active in virtual navigational tasks (see reviews by Maguire, 2001; Spiers and Maguire, 2007; Vann et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: RSC is directly involved in spatial coordinate transformation.
source: In addition, RSC is directly involved in spatial coordinate transformation (Iaria et al., 2007; Epstein, 2008; Hashimoto and Nakano, 2014), which may be crucial for transforming egocentric self-motion signals to allocentric navigational signals in the hippocampal system (Byrne et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A total of 499 single neurons were recorded in the posterior part of the cingulate sulcus above the corpus callosum, including PCC and RSC from five hemispheres of three macaques.
source: A total of 499 single neurons were recorded by single tungsten microelectrode in the posterior part of the cingulate sulcus above the corpus callosum, including the posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) and retrosplenial cortex (RSC) from five hemispheres of three macaques.
evidence: This describes the dataset collected in the study.

claim: 381 units were identified in PCC (Monkey Q: n = 274, monkey P: n = 89, monkey W: n = 18).
source: Among these neurons, 381 units were identified in PCC (Monkey Q: n = 274, monkey P: n = 89, monkey W: n = 18), and 118 units were in RSC (Monkey Q: n = 84, monkey W: n = 34).
evidence: This describes the distribution of recorded neurons across animals.

claim: 118 units were identified in RSC (Monkey Q: n = 84, monkey W: n = 34).
source: Among these neurons, 381 units were identified in PCC (Monkey Q: n = 274, monkey P: n = 89, monkey W: n = 18), and 118 units were in RSC (Monkey Q: n = 84, monkey W: n = 34).
evidence: This describes the distribution of recorded neurons across animals.

claim: In PCC, 68% (252/372) cells were significantly modulated by inertial motion under translation condition.
source: According to this criterion, in PCC, 68% (252/372) cells were significantly modulated by inertial motion under translation condition, whereas 59% (161/271) cells were significantly modulated under the rotation condition (Figure 4A, pie graph and Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by temporal tuning analysis shown in Figure 4A and Table 1.

claim: In PCC, 59% (161/271) cells were significantly modulated under the rotation condition.
source: According to this criterion, in PCC, 68% (252/372) cells were significantly modulated by inertial motion under translation condition, whereas 59% (161/271) cells were significantly modulated under the rotation condition (Figure 4A, pie graph and Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by temporal tuning analysis shown in Figure 4A and Table 1.

claim: About half of the PCC neurons (50%, 131/263) were significantly modulated by both translation and rotation stimuli.
source: About half of the neurons (50%, 131/263) were significantly modulated by both translation and rotation stimuli, indicating that quite a large proportion of PCC neurons received inputs from otolith and semicircular canals at the same time.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of neurons responding to both stimulus types.

claim: A large proportion of PCC neurons received inputs from otolith and semicircular canals at the same time.
source: About half of the neurons (50%, 131/263) were significantly modulated by both translation and rotation stimuli, indicating that quite a large proportion of PCC neurons received inputs from otolith and semicircular canals at the same time.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that many neurons respond to both translation and rotation.

claim: Fewer RSC neurons were significantly modulated under translation (32%, 37/114) and rotation (29%, 25/87) conditions compared to PCC.
source: Compared to PCC, fewer RSC neurons were significantly modulated under translation (32%, 37/114) and rotation (29%, 25/87) conditions (Figure 4A, pie graph).
evidence: This is supported by temporal tuning analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Only 17% (14/83) RSC neurons responded to both translation and rotation stimuli.
source: Only 17% (14/83) RSC neurons responded to both translation and rotation stimuli.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of neurons responding to both stimulus types.

claim: In PCC, 75% (189/252) of temporally tuned neurons showed significant direction tuning under translational condition.
source: We found in PCC, a large proportion of neurons showed significant direction tuning (p<0.01, one-way ANOVA) under translational condition (75%, 189/252) and under rotation condition (77%, 124/161, Figure 4A, bar graph).
evidence: This is supported by spatial tuning analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In PCC, 77% (124/161) of temporally tuned neurons showed significant direction tuning under rotation condition.
source: We found in PCC, a large proportion of neurons showed significant direction tuning (p<0.01, one-way ANOVA) under translational condition (75%, 189/252) and under rotation condition (77%, 124/161, Figure 4A, bar graph).
evidence: This is supported by spatial tuning analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Around 71% (93/131) of PCC neurons were spatially tuned under both translation and rotation conditions.
source: Around 71% (93/131) neurons were spatially tuned under both translation and rotation conditions.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of neurons with spatial tuning in both conditions.

claim: In RSC, only 14% (5/37) and 36% (9/25) neurons were spatially tuned to translation and rotation stimuli, respectively.
source: However, in RSC, only 14% (5/37) and 36% (9/25) neurons were spatially tuned to translation and rotation stimuli, respectively (Figure 4A, bar graph).
evidence: This is supported by spatial tuning analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Only 21% (3/14) of RSC neurons had significant spatial tuning in both translation and rotation conditions.
source: And only 21% (3/14) neurons had significant spatial tuning in both translation and rotation conditions.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of neurons with spatial tuning in both conditions.

claim: The average DDI of all PCC neurons was 0.57 ± 0.007 (mean ± S.E.M.) under the translation condition.
source: The average DDI of all PCC neurons was 0.57 ± 0.007 (mean ± S.E.M.) under the translation condition, and 0.58 ± 0.009 under the rotation condition.
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of spatial tuning strength.

claim: The average DDI of all PCC neurons was 0.58 ± 0.009 under the rotation condition.
source: The average DDI of all PCC neurons was 0.57 ± 0.007 (mean ± S.E.M.) under the translation condition, and 0.58 ± 0.009 under the rotation condition.
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of spatial tuning strength.

claim: For RSC neurons, the average DDI was 0.49 ± 0.013 under translation and 0.50 ± 0.017 under rotation condition.
source: For RSC neurons, the average DDI was 0.49 ± 0.013 and 0.50 ± 0.017 under the translation and rotation condition, respectively, which was significantly weaker compared to that in PCC (p=0.00017 and p=0.0011 for translation and rotation, respectively, t-test).
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of spatial tuning strength with statistical comparison.

claim: RSC neurons carry much weaker vestibular spatial tuning than that in PCC.
source: Thus, neurons in RSC carry much weaker vestibular spatial tuning than that in PCC.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the DDI comparison between PCC and RSC.

claim: Under translation condition, the preferred directions of PCC neurons were distributed almost everywhere in the 3D space, yet there was a tendency that more neurons preferred leftward and rightward motion in the horizontal plane (p=0.01, Uniform test).
source: Under translation condition (Figure 4C, dark blue circles), the preferred directions of PCC neurons were distributed almost everywhere in the 3D space, yet there was a tendency that more neurons preferred leftward and rightward motion in the horizontal plane (p=0.01, Uniform test, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of preferred directions shown in Figure 4C with statistical test.

claim: PCC neurons may be suitable for fine heading discrimination around straight forward during spatial navigation.
source: Such a pattern suggests that PCC neurons may be suitable for fine heading discrimination around straight forward during spatial navigation (Gu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is inferred from the distribution of preferred directions and supported by citation.

claim: Under rotation condition, the preferred rotary axis of PCC neurons concentrated around the horizontal plane (p=0.0225, Uniform test), corresponding to pitch.
source: Interestingly under rotation condition (Figure 4C, light blue triangles), the preferred rotary axis also concentrated around the horizontal plane (p=0.0225, Uniform test), corresponding to pitch (i.e. nose-down or nose-up tilt).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of preferred rotation axes shown in Figure 4C with statistical test.

claim: Majority of PCC neurons showed fairly consistent modulations under fixation and total darkness conditions as indicated by the Pearson's correlation coefficient between the PSTHs in the two conditions.
source: Majority of the neurons showed fairly consistent modulations under the two conditions as indicated by the Pearson's correlation coefficient between the PSTHs in the two conditions (Figure 6A, and see Table 2 for tuning property details).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: DDIs in the fixation and darkness tasks were highly correlated (r = 0.79, p<<0.001, Pearson's correlation), and their mean values were basically the same (p=0.36, paired t-test).
source: Moreover, DDIs in the two tasks were highly correlated (r = 0.79, p<<0.001, Pearson's correlation), and their mean values were basically the same (p=0.36, paired t-test, Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Response strength as indicated by the maximal firing rate had a strong correlation and did not show significant difference between the fixation and darkness tasks (r = 0.80, p<<0.001, Pearson's correlation; p=0.74, paired t-test).
source: Response strength as indicated by the maximal firing rate also had a strong correlation and did not show significant difference between the two tasks (r = 0.80, p<<0.001, Pearson's correlation; p=0.74, paired t-test, Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: None of the neurons tested in the sound control experiment exhibited significant temporal tuning (p>0.01, one-way ANOVA).
source: None of these neurons exhibited significant temporal tuning in the sound control experiment (p>0.01, one-way ANOVA, and see Table 2 for details), and all neurons showed quite weak correlation with the PSTHs in the vestibular condition (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 6D and Table 2.

claim: The vestibular responses observed in the posterior cingulate region are not visual responses due to residual retinal slip.
source: Thus, we exclude the possibility that the vestibular responses observed in the posterior cingulate region are visual responses due to residual retinal slip.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the darkness control experiment results.

claim: The vestibular responses are largely not from an auditory cue.
source: We also largely exclude the possibility from an auditory cue, yet a more thorough investigation covering more factors, such as spatial location, binaural effect, loudness of these cues should be conducted in future studies.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the sound control experiment results, with caveats noted.

claim: Overall, PCC responses were well fitted by VA model in both conditions, with median R2 value of 0.49 for translation and 0.42 for rotation.
source: Overall, PCC responses were well fitted by VA model in both conditions, with median R2 value of 0.49 for translation and 0.42 for rotation.
evidence: This is supported by model fitting results shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Fitting in RSC was worse than PCC (p<<0.001 in both translation and rotation, t-test), with only four neurons and one showing R2 value greater than 0.5 under translational and rotation condition, respectively.
source: However, fitting in RSC was worse (p<<0.001 in both translation and rotation, t-test), with only four neurons and one showing R2 value greater than 0.5 under translational and rotation condition, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by model fitting comparison shown in Figure 8A with statistical test.

claim: In PCC, the log V/A ratio distribution tended to be smaller than 0 under the translational condition (median = −0.21, p<<0.001, Wilcoxon rank sum test).
source: In this area, the log V/A ratio distribution tended to be smaller than 0 under the translational condition (median = −0.21, p<<0.001, Wilcoxon rank sum test), while the distribution tended to be larger than 0 under the rotation condition (median = 0.47, p<<0.001, Wilcoxon rank sum test).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of velocity/acceleration weight ratios shown in Figure 8B.

claim: In PCC, the log V/A ratio distribution tended to be larger than 0 under the rotation condition (median = 0.47, p<<0.001, Wilcoxon rank sum test).
source: In this area, the log V/A ratio distribution tended to be smaller than 0 under the translational condition (median = −0.21, p<<0.001, Wilcoxon rank sum test), while the distribution tended to be larger than 0 under the rotation condition (median = 0.47, p<<0.001, Wilcoxon rank sum test).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of velocity/acceleration weight ratios shown in Figure 8B.

claim: PCC neurons in general carry more acceleration signals in translation condition and more velocity signals in rotation condition.
source: Thus, PCC neurons in general carry more acceleration signals in translation condition and more velocity signals in rotation condition.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the V/A ratio analysis.

claim: The jerk signal is the derivative of acceleration and defines smoothness of the accelerated motion of the head or whole body in the environment.
source: In one of these, the jerk signal is the derivative of acceleration and defines smoothness of the accelerated motion of the head or whole body in the environment.
evidence: This is a definition based on physics and mathematics.

claim: Previous psychophysical and neurophysiological studies have indicated that jerk signal was present in the vestibular afferents and used by subjects to help detect strength of self-motion.
source: Previous psychophysical and neurophysiological studies have indicated that such a signal was present in the vestibular afferents (Fernández and Goldberg, 1976) and used by subjects to help detect strength of self-motion (Benson et al., 1986; Grant and Haycock, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The position signal resulted from the integral of the velocity signal and defines the travelled distance, or rotated head direction, which is critical for path integration.
source: The other is the position signal, resulted from the integral of the velocity signal and defines the travelled distance, or rotated head direction, which is critical for path integration (Etienne and Jeffery, 2004).
evidence: This is a definition with citation to support its importance for path integration.

claim: The full PVAJ model provided better goodness of fit (R2) compared to the VA model across the population (p<<0.001 for both translation and rotation in PCC and RSC, paired t-test).
source: This was also the case across the population (p<<0.001 for both translation and rotation in PCC and RSC, paired t-test, Figure 8A versus Figure 10A).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of model fits shown in Figures 8A and 10A.

claim: Fitting RSC data with the PVAJ model was much worse compared to fitting in PCC (p<<0.001, t-test).
source: However, fitting RSC data with the PVAJ model was much worse compared to fitting in PCC (p<<0.001, t-test, Figure 10A), suggesting that vestibular signals in RSC neurons may not simply follow dynamics defined by the classic temporal components, or may not be as reliable as that in PCC.
evidence: This is supported by model fitting comparison shown in Figure 10A with interpretation.

claim: Majority of PCC neurons exhibited significant and positive partial correlations for all temporal components (p<0.05, Partial correlation).
source: As shown in Figure 10B, majority of neurons exhibited significant and positive partial correlations for all temporal components (p<0.05, Partial correlation).
evidence: This is supported by partial correlation analysis shown in Figure 10B.

claim: After removing the effect of the number of free parameters, BIC value of PVAJ model was still significantly smaller than that of VA model (p<<0.001, Paired t-test).
source: As shown in Figure 10C, after removing the effect of the number of free parameters, BIC value of PVAJ model was still significantly smaller than that of VA model, confirming that including the jerk and position terms did capture more signals embedded in PCC neurons (p<<0.001, Paired t-test).
evidence: This is supported by BIC analysis shown in Figure 10C.

claim: The velocity was more dominant in the rotation condition compared to the other signals which was consistent with that in the VA model.
source: In particular, the velocity was still more dominant in the rotation condition compared to the other signals which was consistent with that in the VA model (red curves in Figure 10D).
evidence: This is supported by weight distribution analysis shown in Figure 10D.

claim: Acceleration and jerk signals weighed more in the translation condition compared to those in the rotation condition.
source: Acceleration and jerk signals weighed more in the translation condition compared to those in the rotation condition (blue and orange curves respectively in Figure 10D).
evidence: This is supported by weight distribution analysis shown in Figure 10D.

claim: The position signal was less dominant compared to the others, particularly in the translation condition.
source: The position signal was less dominant compared to the others, particularly in the translation condition (green curves in Figure 10D).
evidence: This is supported by weight distribution analysis shown in Figure 10D.

claim: MSTd neurons contain robust vestibular signals with velocity-dominant component under translation conditions.
source: Population analysis has indicated that MSTd neurons contain robust vestibular signals with velocity-dominant component under translation conditions (Gu et al., 2006; Laurens et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on MSTd.

claim: Velocity signals tended to be more prevalent in MSTd (VA model: p<<0.001; PVAJ model: p<<0.001, Wilcoxon rank sum test).
source: Consistent with previous findings, Velocity signals tended to be more prevalent in MSTd (VA model: p<<0.001; PVAJ model: p<<0.001, Wilcoxon rank sum test, Figure 11C), a pattern of which was different from that in PCC.
evidence: This is supported by model fitting comparison shown in Figure 11C.

claim: The full model successfully captured more types of signals in PCC than in MSTd (p<<0.001, t-test).
source: Compared between the two areas, BDI analysis revealed that the full model successfully captured more types of signals in PCC than in MSTd (p<<0.001, t-test, Figure 11B, right column).
evidence: This is supported by BDI comparison shown in Figure 11B.

claim: It was mainly the position signal that was more prevalent in PCC compared to that in MSTd (p<<0.001, t-test).
source: A closer examination indicated that it was mainly the position signal that was more prevalent in PCC compared to that in MSTd (p<<0.001, t-test, Figure 11C, right columns, green curves).
evidence: This is supported by weight comparison shown in Figure 11C.

claim: Posterior cingulate neurons reserve self-motion related signals from upstream areas including the extrastriate visual cortex, but the position signal is further developed here, which may be useful for path integration.
source: Thus, this finding suggests that posterior cingulate neurons reserve self-motion related signals from upstream areas including the extrastriate visual cortex, but the position signal is further developed here, which may be useful for path integration.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the comparison between PCC and MSTd.

claim: In PCC, only one third showed significant temporal modulations to optic flow (Translation: 31%, 114/367; Rotation: 32%, 84/260).
source: In PCC, only one third showed significant temporal modulations to optic flow (Translation: 31%, 114/367; Rotation: 32%, 84/260).
evidence: This is supported by visual response analysis shown in Figure 12A and Table 1.

claim: Among PCC cells with significant temporal modulations to optic flow, only one third units showed significant spatial modulations (Translation: 36%, 41/114; Rotation: 24%, 20/84).
source: Furthermore, among those cells with significant temporal modulations, only one third units showed significant (p<0.01, one-way ANOVA) spatial modulations (Translation: 36%, 41/114; Rotation: 24%, 20/84).
evidence: This is supported by visual spatial tuning analysis shown in Figure 12A and Table 1.

claim: In RSC, only about one tenth neurons exhibited significant temporal modulations to visual stimuli (Translation: 11%, 13/114; Rotation: 14%, 12/87).
source: In RSC, visual responses were even negligible. Only about one tenth neurons exhibited significant temporal modulations (Translation: 11%, 13/114; Rotation: 14%, 12/87), among which almost no units presented significant (p<0.01, one-way ANOVA) spatial modulations (Translation: n = 0; Rotation: n = 1).
evidence: This is supported by visual response analysis shown in Figure 12A and Table 1.

claim: Among RSC cells with significant temporal modulations to visual stimuli, almost no units presented significant spatial modulations (Translation: n = 0; Rotation: n = 1).
source: In RSC, visual responses were even negligible. Only about one tenth neurons exhibited significant temporal modulations (Translation: 11%, 13/114; Rotation: 14%, 12/87), among which almost no units presented significant (p<0.01, one-way ANOVA) spatial modulations (Translation: n = 0; Rotation: n = 1).
evidence: This is supported by visual spatial tuning analysis shown in Figure 12A and Table 1.

claim: Across all the cells recorded with an unbiased sampling, the proportion of neurons showing significant spatiotemporal modulations in response to visual heading stimuli was fairly small (~10% in PCC, and ~0% in RSC).
source: Thus, across all the cells recorded with an unbiased sampling (see Materials and methods), the proportion of neurons showing significant spatiotemporal modulations in response to visual heading stimuli was fairly small (~10% in PCC, and ~0% in RSC).
evidence: This is a summary of the visual response findings.

claim: The average visual DDI was much weaker compared to the vestibular DDI in PCC (p<<0.001, t-test).
source: It turned out that the average DDI was much weaker compared to the vestibular DDI in PCC (p<<0.001, t-test), as well as compared to the visual tuning in the extrastriate visual cortex (e.g. MSTd, Gu et al., 2006; Takahashi et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by DDI comparison shown in Figure 12B.

claim: Visual self-motion signals are overall weak in the posterior cingulate region including both PCC and RSC subregions.
source: Hence, visual self-motion signals are overall weak in the posterior cingulate region including both PCC and RSC subregions.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the visual response analysis.

claim: Majority of PCC neurons (~2/3), and a modest proportion (~1/3) of RSC neurons carry robust vestibular linear translation and rotation signals originated from otolith organs and semicircular canals, respectively.
source: In our current study, by recording spiking activities from these areas in macaques during passive physical motions, we provided solid evidence showing that majority of PCC neurons (~2/3), and a modest proportion (~1/3) of RSC neurons carry robust vestibular linear translation and rotation signals originated from otolith organs and semicircular canals, respectively.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the vestibular experiments.

claim: Posterior cingulate cortex is a vestibular dominant region.
source: Surprisingly though, the same region does not appear to carry robust visual self-motion signals such as optic flow or grating, indicating that posterior cingulate cortex is a vestibular dominant region.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the comparison of vestibular and visual responses.

claim: Smith et al., 2012 reported clear vestibular signals in a homologues area (cingulate sulcus visual area, CSv) in the human brain.
source: For example, Smith et al., 2012 reported clear vestibular signals in a homologues area (cingulate sulcus visual area, CSv) in the human brain.
evidence: This is a citation to a previous fMRI study.

claim: Caloric or galvanic stimulation techniques can only activate the vestibular system in a general way, instead of being able to simulate real and accurate self-motion including translation along certain directions or rotation around specific axis in 3D environment.
source: In particular, caloric or galvanic stimulation techniques can only activate the vestibular system in a general way (Suzuki et al., 2001; Fitzpatrick and Day, 2004; Utz et al., 2010), instead of being able to simulate real and accurate self-motion including translation along certain directions or rotation around specific axis in 3D environment.
evidence: This is a limitation of previous methods noted with citations.

claim: Vestibular signals typically carry complex temporal dynamics (i.e. in milliseconds) that cannot be easily captured by BOLD signals with a relatively slow temporal resolution (i.e. in seconds).
source: Moreover, vestibular signals typically carry complex temporal dynamics (i.e. in milliseconds) that cannot be easily captured by BOLD signals with a relatively slow temporal resolution (i.e. in seconds).
evidence: This is a known limitation of fMRI compared to electrophysiology.

claim: There is a rough consistency between spiking activity from single neurons with BOLD signals.
source: In general, we found robust vestibular signals in similar regions as indicated in previous imaging studies (yet with more spatiotemporal information as discussed in the following sections), confirming a rough consistency between spiking activity from single neurons with BOLD signals (Berens et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a comparison between the current findings and previous fMRI studies with citation.

claim: The posterior cingulate region is more involved in more complex environment when visual stimuli are ever-changing.
source: It is possible that the posterior cingulate region is more involved in more complex environment when visual stimuli are ever-changing.
evidence: This is speculation to explain discrepancies with previous visual response studies.

claim: Direct inputs of vestibular signals to PCC originate from a number of sources, including the thalamus, the parietal insular vestibular cortex (PIVC), and the parietal-temporal cortices.
source: Direct inputs of vestibular signals to PCC originate from a number of sources, including the thalamus (Shinder and Taube, 2010), the parietal insular vestibular cortex (PIVC) (Guldin and Grüsser, 1998), and the parietal-temporal cortices (Pandya et al., 1981; Vogt et al., 1987; Musil and Olson, 1988; Cavada and Goldman-Rakic, 1989; Olson and Musil, 1992; Akbarian et al., 1994; Shinder and Taube, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical connectivity studies.

claim: PCC is one of the nodes within the cortical vestibular network.
source: In the current study, we also found clear temporal and spatial modulations in a large proportion of neurons in PCC, with many properties qualitatively similar to those in the insular and parietal-temporal areas, indicating PCC is one of the nodes within the cortical vestibular network.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity of response properties to other vestibular areas.

claim: Information theory predicts that a pattern of distributed preferred directions biased toward leftward and rightward motion is useful for detection of fine-varied headings around straight ahead.
source: Information theory predicts that such a pattern of distributed preferred directions is useful for detection of fine-varied headings around straight ahead (Gu et al., 2010), suggesting that PCC could be involved in heading perception.
evidence: This is supported by citation to information theory analysis.

claim: In mice, azimuth-tuning of head direction cells is affixed to the head-horizontal plane when the animals' head positions were changed relative to gravity.
source: A previous study has reported that in mice, azimuth-tuning of head direction cells is affixed to the head-horizontal plane when the animals' head positions were changed relative to gravity (Angelaki et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Rotation signals in PCC could be essential for head direction cells to function properly in 3D environments.
source: Therefore, these rotation signals could be essential for head direction cells to function properly in 3D environments.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding about preferred rotation axes and cited study on HD cells.

claim: A process of integrating the velocity quantity to position may happen in PCC when self-motion related information is propagated closer to the hippocampus system.
source: According to weight value, this component is less dominant compared to the others, but is more prevalent than that in the extrastriate visual cortex, suggesting that a process of integrating the velocity quantity to position may happen in PCC when self-motion related information is propagated closer to the hippocampus system.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of position signal prevalence between PCC and MSTd.

claim: PCC directly sends signals back to the vestibular nucleus (VN) in brainstem.
source: As to the outputs of PCC, it also directly sends signals back to the vestibular nucleus (VN) in brainstem (Akbarian et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to anatomical study.

claim: The pathway from PCC to vestibular nucleus may be involved in gaze control or other reflex behaviors during coordinated eye, head, and body movements during natural navigation.
source: This pathway may be involved in gaze control or other reflex behaviors during coordinated eye, head, and body movements during natural navigation (Dean and Platt, 2006; Shinder and Taube, 2010).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations.

claim: Vestibular signals with rich temporal and spatial information in PCC may compose a high and mixed dimensional neural representation that could be used by downstream neurons through a simple, linear readout algorithm to compute an efficient and flexible variable according to ongoing task's need.
source: Instead, vestibular signals with rich temporal and spatial information in PCC may compose a high and mixed dimensional neural representation that could be used by downstream neurons through a simple, linear readout algorithm to compute an efficient and flexible variable according to ongoing task's need.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the functional role of PCC signals.

claim: PCC is reciprocally connected with PIVC that in turn receives projections from the viscera system through the solitary tract and the parabrachial complex.
source: PCC is also reciprocally connected with PIVC that in turn receives projections from the viscera system through the solitary tract and the parabrachial complex (Vogt, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to anatomical connectivity study.

claim: Electrical stimulation in PIVC evokes unpleasant emotions including vomiting, nausea, dizziness, and pain.
source: Electrical stimulation in PIVC evokes unpleasant emotions including vomiting, nausea, dizziness, and pain (Penfield and Faulk, 1955; Penfield, 1957; Mazzola et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to stimulation studies.

claim: Vestibular signals in PCC may also be related to emotion.
source: Thus, vestibular signals in PCC may also be related to emotion, which requires further investigations in the future.
evidence: This is speculation based on connectivity with emotion-related areas.

claim: PCC neurons contain spatial choice and reward-target signals in a complex, adaptive task.
source: For example, in a recent study, Gold and his colleagues reported that PCC neurons contain spatial choice and reward-target signals in a complex, adaptive task (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: Vestibular yaw-rotation signals have been observed in mice RSC.
source: Vestibular yaw-rotation signals have been observed in mice RSC (Keshavarzi et al., 2021), as well as primary visual cortex (V1) which may originate directly from RSC as revealed by tracing and functional mapping (Vélez-Fort et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study in mice.

claim: Mice RSC receives heavy inputs from V1 as well as other sensory information related with spatial perception, suggesting RSC is a multisensory area albeit biased toward visual.
source: At the same time, mice RSC also receives heavy inputs from V1 as well as other sensory information related with spatial perception, suggesting RSC is a multisensory area albeit biased toward visual (Zingg et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to connectivity study in mice.

claim: Visual responses modulated by grating stimuli were reported in mice RSC.
source: Recently, Powell and colleagues also reported visual responses modulated by grating stimuli in mice RSC (Powell et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study in mice.

claim: Lesion of RSC significantly impaired mice's performance during spatial navigation when they relied on visual landmarks but not much when animals were required to rely on self-motion cues.
source: For example, lesion of RSC significantly impaired mice's performance during spatial navigation when they relied on visual landmarks but not much when animals were required to rely on self-motion cues (Clark et al., 2010; Mitchell et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to lesion studies in mice.

claim: RSC may not be much involved in vector-based navigation particularly when relying optic flow to update one's self-motion directions or travelled distance.
source: Thus, RSC may not be much involved in vector-based navigation particularly when relying optic flow to update one's self-motion directions or travelled distance.
evidence: This is inferred from lesion studies and the current findings.

claim: Homologous areas of RSC across species could be somehow different and execute heterogeneous functions to adapt to environments during evolution.
source: Thus, homologous areas across species could be somehow different and execute heterogeneous functions to adapt to environments during evolution.
evidence: This is speculation about species differences.

claim: Temporal component signals in RSC may either be less reliable, or more complex that need other models to be further developed to better capture the data.
source: Moreover, the same 3D spatiotemporal model does not fit data in RSC as well as that in PCC, suggesting that temporal component signals in RSC may either be less reliable, or more complex that need other models to be further developed to better capture the data.
evidence: This is inferred from the poor model fits in RSC.

claim: Macaque PCC and RSC may contribute to spatial navigation in different ways.
source: In any case, our results suggest that macaque PCC and RSC may contribute to spatial navigation in different ways.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differences in response properties between PCC and RSC.

source: By estimation, the peak velocity was ~0.3 m/s and the peak acceleration was 1 m/s2 in the translation condition.
evidence: This describes the stimulus parameters used in the experiments.

source: In the rotation condition, the peak angular velocity was ~20 °/s and the peak acceleration was 60°/s2.
evidence: This describes the stimulus parameters used in the experiments.

source: The overall response delay (τ) was around 0 ms.
